title: The freedom of a Christian
hook: Luther: a Christian is free lord of all, and dutiful servant of all

segments.voice: Yesterday, Julian of Norwich and God our mother. Your line was our true mother.

Two sentences, side by side, that seem to cancel each other out. A Christian is a free lord of all, subject to no one. A Christian is a dutiful servant of all, subject to everyone. Martin Luther, whose hammer you met in year one, set those two at the top of a short book called The Freedom of a Christian, and spent the rest of it showing why both are true at once. Free and bound. Lord and servant. It sounds like a riddle.

Luther's freedom starts somewhere unexpected: not with what a person does, but with what a person receives. For Luther, someone is made right with God by faith, by trusting God's promise in Christ, not by piling up good works. That's the lord-of-all half. In Luther's telling, nothing a person fails at can take away what God has given, and nobody is working to earn their place. So the Christian is free. Then comes the turn. Free for what? Luther's answer: for the neighbor. Because Christians don't need good works to save themselves, they can give those works away. Works stop being a ladder you climb and become a gift you hand across the fence. He took the pattern from Paul: "For though I be free from all men, yet have I made myself servant unto all." And again: "Owe no man any thing, but to love one another." To the Galatians, Paul puts both halves in one breath: "ye have been called unto liberty; only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another." Luther even pictures a Christian becoming a kind of Christ to the neighbor, giving freely as Christ gave. Christians describe faith and works in different ways. Lutheran churches follow Luther closely here. Catholic and Orthodox Christians also teach that grace comes first and that love must act, while explaining how faith and works fit together in their own terms. In each of them, the neighbor still gets served.

Bring to mind one small service for someone who can't pay you back and might not even notice: a neighbor's bin, a coworker's extra task, the dish someone left in the sink. Watch where your mind goes, will they thank me, will it count, and let those questions drop, picturing it done out of freedom, with nothing to earn. If you pray, you can offer it to God.
The freedom of a Christian. Luther's two sentences: free lord of all, through faith; dutiful servant of all, through love.

fork.setup: a friend has just heard that nothing anyone does can earn God's love; it's a gift. they ask: so why bother doing good at all? what would Luther say?
options: "you don't need to; faith is enough, so stop."
"because you're free, you can give your good works to your neighbor."
"do them to make sure you're really saved."
fork.reveal: free lord of all, through faith; dutiful servant of all, through love. good works stop being a ladder and become a gift.

chat.says: If Luther says faith makes you free, why bother doing good for anyone?
options: Luther says you're free for your neighbor: good works aren't a ladder to climb but a gift.
Luther says the two sentences can't both be true, so he chose servant over free.
Luther says faith frees you from others, so serving neighbors is optional extra credit.
chat.meaning: For Luther, a Christian is free by faith, and that freedom is for the neighbor: works become a gift handed across the fence, given freely.

notes: Luther's two theses are paraphrased (the 1883 Wace and Buchheim translation is public domain but not on the validator's list).
'A kind of Christ to the neighbor' paraphrases a well-known line in the treatise; confirm.
Catholic and Orthodox views on faith and works are summarized in one sentence; a scholar should confirm it is fair to each.
Galatians 5:13 Greek ἐλευθερία is given in the dictionary form; the verse has ἐπ᾽ ἐλευθερίᾳ.
